description: We are a team of high school students passionate about computer science, artificial intelligence, and space exploration. Our goal is to create an innovative solution using NASA's open data and modern technology. We enjoy programming, problem-solving, and building useful applications. We will collaborate virtually to develop and present our project.
summary: Solar Storm Outpost is a free web game that trains kids to run a Moon or Mars base for 14 days during real space weather. Every solar flare, CME, and particle storm in the game comes from NASA's DONKI database, either live from the last 14 days or from saved real storm windows like September 2017. Players protect their crew with shields and shelter drills, and every number on screen is tagged as Real data, Estimate, or Game number so kids learn what is real science and what is a game rule.
details:
Players pick the Moon or Mars, then a data window: live DONKI data from the last 14 days or one of four saved real windows (Oct 2026, May 2024, Sep 2017, Dec 2023). Each day shows a real event card with the date, flare class, UTC time, active region, and CME speed, with links to the DONKI record. Players then play in one of two modes. In Astronaut mode they move around a top-down 2D base, placing power cells and running to shelter during storm drills. In Command dials mode they set four dials for power, shields, air, and food, then run the day. After 14 days a mission report scores the run, compares the crew radiation dose to real measured rates, and lists what went right and wrong. It is built as a web app hosted on Vercel and pulls DONKI flare, CME, and SEP data from the NASA API. Our goal was to make space weather something kids can feel and understand, using real NASA data instead of made-up storms.

Use of AI: We used Claude Code (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant to help with the frontend design of web app and an AI assistant to QA test the game, we wrote most of the backend code by our selves. We also used Codex as a coding helper, and AI tools helped draft the plain language Why cards and check the reading level. We designed the game, chose the data, and checked every number ourselves. AI tools did not invent any space data, and every made-up game rule is labelled Game number.
